reproduction.text: Gives birth to live young, often 10-20

overview.text: The Common Gartersnake is one of North America's most widespread snakes, found across most of the non-desert parts of the continent, and it reaches farther north than any other North American snake. It is not dangerous to people and copes with cold better than most snakes.

identification.text: Most have yellowish stripes along a black, brown or green body, but the colours vary a great deal - including green, blue, gold, red and orange forms.

size.label: Adults
size.text: In South Dakota adults measure about 46 to 76 cm (18 to 30 in). Few grow longer than about 1.2 m; the maximum given is about 137 cm.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: Much of North America, from the south of Canada through most of the non-desert United States.

habitat.text: Usually close to water: along rivers, lakes and reservoirs, in wetlands and in the strips of plants beside streams. It also turns up at forest edges and even in vacant lots in towns, but is rarely found in dry places far from water.

behaviour.text: Mostly active by day. It handles colder temperatures than many snakes and may even bask on rocks on mild winter days.

behaviour.label: Winter
behaviour.text: Gartersnakes hibernate in large groups and mate in spring as they come out of their winter dens. In Manitoba, Canada, the huge spring gatherings of the Red-sided Gartersnake at Narcisse draw visitors from around the world.
It finds prey mainly by smell and sight, sometimes waiting in ambush. It does not squeeze (constrict) its prey: it grabs it and quickly swallows it whole.
behaviour.label: Hunting

diet.text: Mainly frogs, toads and salamanders, but a wide range of other prey has been recorded, from earthworms and fish to voles.

teeth.text: It subdues prey with its teeth and quick reflexes. Its saliva may be mildly toxic to some small prey, which makes them easier to handle.

reproduction.text: It gives birth to live young in late summer and autumn - no eggs are laid. Most litters are of about 10 to 20 young, but large females can have many more (up to about 80 have been recorded). Newborns are about 15 to 20 cm long.

recognise.text: Three light stripes: one down the middle of the back and one low on each side, on the second and third rows of scales up from the belly.
Between the stripes the body is dark - black, brown, grey or green - often with rows of dark spots; some have red between the scales on the sides.
A pale belly - whitish, light yellow or grey-green - with dark spots along the edges of the belly scales.
Keeled scales (a ridge down each one), faint black bars on the upper lip and round pupils.
Colours vary a great deal: besides the usual yellowish stripes there are green, blue, gold, red and orange forms.
recognise.label: Colour forms

funfacts.text: No other North American snake lives as far north as the Common Gartersnake.
